cards.prompt: Compare encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder transformers: attention pattern, pretraining, best tasks, and examples.

keyPoints.text: Encoder-only: attention sees the whole sentence (bidirectional); also called auto-encoding
Encoder pretraining usually corrupts a sentence (e.g. masks words) and has the model reconstruct it
Encoders suit understanding the full input: sentence classification, named entity recognition, extractive QA (e.g. BERT)
Decoder-only: each word attends only to earlier words; auto-regressive; pretrained to predict the next word; suited to generation (e.g. Llama, Gemma)
Encoder-decoder (seq2seq): bidirectional encoder plus a decoder that sees only earlier positions
Seq2seq suits generating text from an input: summarization, translation, generative QA (e.g. T5, BART)
T5 pretraining replaces random spans with a single mask token and predicts the span

cards.explanation: To choose: ask whether the task needs bidirectional understanding, whether you're generating or analyzing text, and whether you're transforming one sequence into another.

cards.prompt: Which architecture do most modern LLMs use, and what are the two phases they're typically trained in?

keyPoints.text: Most modern LLMs are decoder-only
Phase 1, pretraining: predict the next token over vast amounts of text
Phase 2, instruction tuning: fine-tune the model to follow instructions and give helpful responses

cards.explanation: Some of the largest of these models have hundreds of billions of parameters.

cards.prompt: LLM inference runs in two phases. Describe prefill and decode, and whether each is compute- or memory-intensive.

keyPoints.text: Prefill: tokenize the input, convert tokens to embeddings, and run them through the model
Prefill processes all input tokens at once, so it is compute-intensive
Decode: generate one token at a time, autoregressively (each token depends on all previous ones)
Each decode step: attend over previous tokens, compute next-token probabilities, pick a token, decide whether to stop
Decode is memory-intensive because it keeps track of all previous tokens

cards.explanation: A useful mental model: prefill is reading the whole prompt, decode is writing the answer word by word.

cards.prompt: How do temperature, top-p, and top-k shape token selection? How do you control repetition and output length?

keyPoints.text: The model starts with raw probabilities (logits) for every word in its vocabulary
Temperature above 1 makes choices more random; below 1, more focused and deterministic
Top-p (nucleus): consider only the most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to a threshold (e.g. 90%)
Top-k: consider only the k most likely tokens
Presence penalty: a fixed penalty on any token that already appeared; frequency penalty grows with how often it appeared
Penalties adjust raw probabilities before other sampling steps
Length controls: min/max token limits, stop sequences, and end-of-sequence detection

cards.explanation: Example from the course: for a single paragraph, cap at about 100 tokens and use a blank line ("\n\n") as a stop sequence.

cards.prompt: What is beam search, how does it work, and what does it trade off?

keyPoints.text: Instead of committing to one token per step, it explores several candidate sequences at once
Keep multiple candidates per step (typically 5–10)
Score next tokens for each candidate and keep only the most promising combinations
Repeat until the length limit or a stop condition, then pick the sequence with the highest overall probability
Often more coherent and grammatical, but costs more compute

cards.explanation: Contrast with sampling strategies, which decide one token at a time.

cards.prompt: Name four key metrics for LLM inference performance and what each one affects.

keyPoints.text: Time to first token (TTFT): how fast the first output appears; mainly driven by prefill
Time per output token (TPOT): speed of generating subsequent tokens; sets overall generation speed
Throughput: how many requests you can handle at once; affects scaling and cost
VRAM usage: GPU memory needed; often the main real-world constraint

cards.explanation: The source frames these four as the metrics that shape implementation decisions; of them, TTFT is the one it calls crucial for user experience.

cards.prompt: What is context length, what does a long context cost, and how does KV caching help?

keyPoints.text: Context length: the maximum number of tokens the model can consider at once (its working memory)
It's limited by model architecture and size, compute resources, and input/output complexity
Longer context: memory usage grows quadratically and processing gets slower
Very long context windows (e.g. 1M tokens) come with much slower inference
KV (key-value) caching stores and reuses intermediate calculations instead of recomputing them
KV caching speeds up generation and makes long contexts practical, at the cost of extra memory

cards.explanation: Different models pick different context lengths to balance capability against efficiency.
